chapters.title: Google, Meet OKRs
chapters.sourcePressure: Google has ambition, capital, and technology, but Doerr introduces OKRs as the execution discipline that turns scale pressure into visible priorities and proof.
chapters.coreMove: Separate the ambition from the evidence by naming one objective and the key results that would prove it is moving.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not reduce the opening to generic goal setting or startup inspiration.

chapters.title: The Father of OKRs
chapters.sourcePressure: Andy Grove is the origin of OKRs: the method carries Intel managerial rigor around ownership, clarity, and measurable follow-through.
chapters.coreMove: Turn a respected goal into an owned and testable commitment before discussion can blur into approval theater.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not portray Grove as merely strict or the method as a tidy acronym.

chapters.title: Operation Crush: An Intel Story
chapters.sourcePressure: Operation Crush shows Intel under competitive threat, rapidly rebooting priorities while field signals from people like Don Buckout and Casey Powell move upward.
chapters.coreMove: In a crisis, reduce the noise to one company-level fight and keep a clean path for bad news to correct the plan.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not claim panic creates excellence or invent extra competitive battle scenes.

chapters.title: Superpower #1: Focus and Commit to Priorities
chapters.sourcePressure: The first superpower makes focus and commitment explicit: choose what matters most and win enough participation that chosen priorities govern action.
chapters.coreMove: Make worthy alternatives lose so the surviving priorities can command time, resources, and buy-in.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not make focus sound like personal minimalism or commitment like verbal agreement.

chapters.title: Focus: The Remind Story
chapters.sourcePressure: Remind is the company case for focus, showing why a smaller number of decisive moves must be protected from overload.
chapters.coreMove: Demote respectable extras and defend the few strategic moves that actually lead execution.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not invent Remind product metrics or internal scenes; keep it as a focus case.

chapters.title: Commit: The Nuna Story
chapters.sourcePressure: Nuna is the company case for commitment, showing that buy-in means chosen priorities must govern calendars, tradeoffs, and effort.
chapters.coreMove: Test commitment by identifying what old obligation lost power after the priority was chosen.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not treat commitment as morale, loyalty, or public enthusiasm.

chapters.title: Superpower #2: Align and Connect for Teamwork
chapters.sourcePressure: The second superpower introduces alignment and connection: visible priorities create shared direction and expose dependencies across teams.
chapters.coreMove: Draw the shared map before teams optimize locally and collide later.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not make alignment mean forced sameness or more communication meetings.

chapters.title: Align: The MyFitnessPal Story
chapters.sourcePressure: MyFitnessPal is the company case for alignment, with support only for connected priorities, dependency visibility, and silo drift.
chapters.coreMove: Use linked priorities to make cross-team execution visible before local work pulls apart.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not invent MyFitnessPal internal product detail, metrics, or management biography.

chapters.title: Connect: The Intuit Story
chapters.sourcePressure: Intuit is the company case for connection, emphasizing real linkage across work rather than disconnected parallel effort.
chapters.coreMove: Turn adjacent workstreams into explicit handoffs so parallel effort becomes connected execution.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not make connection a synonym for friendliness, chat volume, or meeting frequency.

chapters.title: Superpower #3: Track for Accountability
chapters.sourcePressure: The third superpower introduces tracking and accountability as live visibility, course correction, and owned progress.
chapters.coreMove: Make progress reviewable early enough that teams can correct drift before excuses harden.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not frame tracking as surveillance, punishment, or neat reporting.

chapters.title: Track: The Gates Foundation Story
chapters.sourcePressure: The Gates Foundation is the named case for tracking, where progress must stay visible enough for review, correction, and ownership.
chapters.coreMove: Use reviewable movement to separate accountable correction from explanation after the fact.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not invent foundation programs, metrics, grants, or internal meeting scenes.

chapters.title: Superpower #4: Stretch for Amazing
chapters.sourcePressure: The fourth superpower introduces stretch: ambitious reach beyond safe incremental targets, held by effort and accountability.
chapters.coreMove: Raise the ceiling without cutting the tether to evidence, effort, and ownership.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not make stretch mean fantasy targets, hustle rhetoric, or reckless overpromising.

chapters.title: Stretch: The Google Chrome Story
chapters.sourcePressure: Google Chrome is the company case for stretch, with narrow support for bold targets and grounded accountability but no internal launch detail.
chapters.coreMove: Set a bold reach target that forces stronger execution without becoming hype.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not invent Chrome launch metrics, product tactics, or management scenes.

chapters.title: Stretch: The YouTube Story
chapters.sourcePressure: YouTube is a second company case for stretch, proving ambitious reach has to remain grounded across more than one surface.
chapters.coreMove: Use a second proof case to test whether stretch stays disciplined when the target gets louder.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not invent YouTube growth metrics, creator details, or internal product decisions.

chapters.title: Continuous Performance Management: OKRs and CFRs
chapters.sourcePressure: Part 2 pairs OKRs with continuous performance management and CFRs: conversation, feedback, and recognition around living goals.
chapters.coreMove: Add a live support loop around the objective so performance improves while the work can still change.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not import the Adobe case yet or turn CFRs into generic kindness.

chapters.title: Ditching Annual Performance Reviews: The Adobe Story
chapters.sourcePressure: Adobe is the named case for moving beyond annual performance reviews toward ongoing conversation, feedback, and recognition.
chapters.coreMove: Move the performance signal forward from delayed ritual to live support around the work.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not invent Adobe policy mechanics, metrics, or leadership biography.

chapters.title: Baking Better Every Day: The Zume Pizza Story
chapters.sourcePressure: Zume Pizza is the named case for better-every-day logic: repeated betterment, live feedback, and ongoing adjustment.
chapters.coreMove: Pull feedback close enough to execution that the work gets better before rescue is required.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not invent Zume robotics, logistics, pizza operations, or metrics.

chapters.title: Culture
chapters.sourcePressure: The culture chapter widens Part 2 from company cases into the environment made by repeated signals, reinforcement, accountability, conversation, feedback, and recognition.
chapters.coreMove: Read culture from the signals people repeatedly experience, not from the values language they hear.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not make culture a vibe, perk package, or slogan exercise.

chapters.title: Culture Change: The Lumeris Story
chapters.sourcePressure: Lumeris is the company case for culture change, focused on changed norms, expectations, reinforcement, and accountability over time.
chapters.coreMove: Prove culture change by tracing which repeated signals retrain expectations in practice.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not invent Lumeris policies, product details, metrics, or leaders.

chapters.title: Culture Change: Bono's ONE Campaign Story
chapters.sourcePressure: Bono and the ONE Campaign extend culture-change logic into a mission-driven organization, where purpose language still cannot substitute for changed norms.
chapters.coreMove: Test whether a noble mission has changed the operating pattern underneath the message.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not invent ONE Campaign tactics, politics, fundraising, or internal programs.

chapters.title: The Goals to Come
chapters.sourcePressure: The closing chapter points toward future goals and asks the reader to carry the operating logic forward with structure, measurement, support, and responsibility.
chapters.coreMove: Drag the next future goal into an operating system before admiration can decay into drift.
chapters.commonMisread: Do not close with empty inspiration or introduce unsupported new anecdotes.
